parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech acht, possibly from Middle High German āhte.

Borrowed from Middle High German almuosen, from Old High German alamuosa, from Proto-West Germanic *alemōsinā, borrowed from Vulgar Latin *alēmosyna, from Late Latin eleēmosyna, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐλεημοσύνη (eleēmosúnē), from ἐλεήμων (eleḗmōn, “pitiful, merciful”) + -σῠ́νη (-sŭ́nē). First
Inherited from Old Czech anýž, from Middle High German anīs, from Latin anisum, from Ancient Greek ἄνισον (ánison).
Borrowed from Middle High German varwe. Compare modern German Farbe, Dutch verf, Polish barwa, Polish farba.

parole.significato: cotton (the textile made from the fiber harvested from the cotton plant)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech bavlna, borrowed from Middle High German boumwolle, whence German Baumwolle. The word is a partial calque, the second part having been assimilated to vlna (“wool”).
Inherited from Old Czech bažant, from Middle High German vasant, from Latin phasianus, from Ancient Greek φασιανός (phasianós).
Inherited from Old Czech berla, from Middle High German ferla.

parole.significato: to blink, twinkle (of a source of light)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle High German blicken (“to look”, originally "to shine").

First known occurrence of the expression in the Czech language (16th century) was in the sense side (of a gutter or hole). From early Middle High German bord, bort ("side", especially of a ship; originally "a board", "a plank"). This comes from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerH- (“cut”).
Inherited from Old Czech buda, from Middle High German buode, from Proto-Germanic *bōþō (whence English booth).

parole.significato: bun or piece of bread long in shape
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech calta, from Middle High German zëlte.
Borrowed from Middle High German zëch(e); see modern German Zeche.

Inherited from Old Czech cajch, cejch. Borrowed from Middle High German zeichen, from Old High German zeihhan, from Proto-West Germanic *taikn, from Proto-Germanic *taikną, from Proto-Indo-European *deyḱ- (“to point out”). First attested in the 14th century.
Inherited from Old Czech chvíle, from Middle High German wīle, from Old High German wīla, from Proto-West Germanic *hwīlu. Cognates include Ukrainian хвили́на (xvylýna).
Inherited from Old Czech cibule, from Middle High German zwibolle, from Late Latin cēpulla, from Latin cēpa.
Inherited from Old Czech cimbořie, from Middle High German zibōrje, from Latin cibōrium. Other theories include German Zinnenburg.

parole.significato: duty, tariff, customs duty (on export and import)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech clo, borrowed from Middle High German zol.

parole.significato: to back (to go in the reverse direction)
parole.testo: Derived from Middle High German zaufen. Compare Polish cofać, Pannonian Rusyn цофац (cofac).

parole.significato: to exercise (to perform activities to develop skills)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle High German zwicken, from Old High German *zwicchēn. Cognate with German zwicken, English twitch.

parole.significato: short, stocky person, esp. a child
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech cvok, cvek (“iron nail”). Borrowed from Middle High German zwëc, wherefrom German zwicken. The change in the meaning comes from the idiom mít cvek v hlavě (“to be a nutcase”).
Inherited from Old Czech cícha, ciecha. Borrowed from Middle High German zieche.
Inherited from Old Czech cíl, from Middle High German zil. Compare German Ziel.
Inherited from Old Czech cíp, from Middle High German zipf (compare German Zipfel).

Inherited from Old Czech datel, from Middle High German datel, from Ancient Greek δάκτυλος (dáktulos) ("a date", but also "a finger"), which is probably of Semitic origin; compare Arabic دَقَل (daqal) (variety of date palm).
Inherited from Old Czech deka, from Middle High German decke.

parole.significato: warrant officer, catchpole (officer assigned to collect debts, etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech dráb, from Middle High German drabant, trabant.
Inherited from Old Czech diek, from Middle High German danc, from Proto-Germanic *þankaz.
Inherited from Old Czech déka, borrowed from Late Middle High German dege(n). See German Degen for more.
Derived from Middle High German esse n (“a single point on a die”).
Borrowed from Middle High German valde, from Old High German faldan.
Inherited from Old Czech forman, from Middle High German vuorman. See German Fuhrmann.
Inherited from Old Czech fortna, from Middle High German phorte (“gate”), from Latin porta (“gate”).
From Middle High German forster (modern German Förster).
Inherited from Old Czech fěrtuch, from Middle High German vortuoch (today German Fürtuch).
Inherited from Old Czech grunt, from Middle High German grunt, from Old High German grunt (modern German Grund).
Borrowed from Middle High German haller, from Schwäbisch Hall, the town where they were minted.

parole.significato: habit (often worn by monks or nuns)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech hazuka, from Middle High German husecke.
Inherited from Old Czech hedvábie. Probably from Middle High German gota-webbi (“god cloth, cloth for religious use”) (compare German Gott (“god”), weben (“to weave”)).

parole.significato: mortar (a hollow vessel used to pound, crush, rub, grind or mix ingredients with a pestle)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech moždieř, from Middle High German mörser, ultimately from Latin mortārium. Reanalysed as hmoždit + -íř.
Inherited from Old Czech hold, from Middle High German hulde (German Huld).
Inherited from Old Czech hont, from Middle High German gant, from Latin canthērius.
Inherited from Old Czech húf, hauf. Borrowed from Middle High German hufe (“heap”), from Old High German hūfo.
Inherited from Old Czech hrabie, itself borrowed from Middle High German grâve, from Old High German grāfio (“ruler”) (German Graf).
Inherited from Old Czech hut, from Middle High German hütte (modern German Hütte).
Inherited from Old Czech hák, from Middle High German hāken, from Old High German hāko (“hook”); cognate with German Haken and English hook.
Inherited from Old Czech hýřiti. Possibly borrowed from Middle High German irren.
Inherited from Old Czech břitov, from Middle High German frithof. Reanalysed as hřbít + -ov.
Inherited from Old Czech jilec, from Middle High German gehilze. Compare English hilt.
Inherited from Old Czech kacieř, from Middle High German ketzer.
Inherited from Old Czech kalich, kelich, from Middle High German kelich (German Kelch).
Inherited from Old Czech kapitán (“deputy of a king”), from Middle High German kapitān, from Medieval Latin capitāneus, from Latin caput.
Borrowed from Middle High German knöfel.
Inherited from Old Czech knot, from Middle High German knote, knode.
Inherited from Old Czech koflík, from deminutive of Middle High German kopf (compare German Kopf). Compare hoblík, rendlík, žejdlík, truhlík.
Inherited from Old Czech komňata, from Middle High German chomenate, from Latin camīnāta.

parole.significato: larder, pantry, closet, boxroom or utility room
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech komora, from Middle High German kamara.
Inherited from Old Czech, borrowed from Middle High German kanne (“jug, pitcher, can”), whence also Slovak kanva, Polish konew, Ukrainian кíнва (kínva), Russian ко́новь (kónovʹ).
Inherited from Old Czech korba, from Middle High German korp (German Korb), from Latin corbis. Related to krabice inherited from Proto-Slavic.
Inherited from Old Czech kule, kúle, from Middle High German kūle, kugele, see German Kugel (“ball”).
Borrowed from Middle High German kost(e), from Medieval Latin *costus.
From Middle High German kirchhof.
Inherited from Old Czech kredenc, from Middle High German crēdenz, from Italian credenza.
Inherited from Old Czech krajcar, from Middle High German kriuzer.
Inherited from Old Czech krychle, from Middle High German krichelîn.
Borrowed from Middle High German Kram (“cloth on display, merchant tent”) of uncertain origin.
Derived from Middle High German kurvürste.

parole.significato: chrism (mixture of oil and balm, consecrated for use as an anointing fluid in certain Christian ceremonies, especially…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech křižmo, from Middle High German chrismo, from Latin chrīsma, from Ancient Greek χρῖσμα (khrîsma).
Borrowed from Middle High German krīde, from Latin crēta.
Inherited from Old Czech kšaft. Borrowed from Middle High German gescheft. Doublet of kšeft.
Inherited from Old Czech lampa, from Middle High German lampe (compare German Lampe), from Latin lampas, from Ancient Greek λαμπάς (lampás).

Derived from Middle High German lanne (“chain”), from Old High German lanna (“metal sheet, platelet; chain”), from Vulgar Latin lanna from Latin lāmina (“sheet especially of metal”). Cognate with Serbo-Croatian ла́нац (“chain”), Slovene lanec (“chain”), Macedonian and Bulgarian ланец (lanec, “golden
Inherited from Old Czech lat, from Middle High German latte (compare German Latte).

parole.significato: leopard (a large wild cat with a spotted coat, Panthera pardus)
parole.testo: Derived from Middle High German lëwpart, lēparte. Compare Polish lampart.
Inherited from Old Czech ľubček, from Middle High German lübestecke.
Inherited from Old Czech lišta, from Middle High German līste.
Inherited from Old Czech lúbie, from Middle High German loube (German Laube).
From Middle High German lēhen, from Old High German lēhan, from Proto-Germanic *laihną.
From Old Czech man, from Middle High German and Old High German man.
Inherited from Old Czech ma(r)štal, ma(r)štale, from Middle High German marstal. See German Marstall.

Inherited from Old Czech mišpile, mišpule, from Middle High German mispel, from Old High German mespila, from Proto-West Germanic *mespilā, from Latin mespilum, mespila, from Ancient Greek μέσπιλον (méspilon).

parole.significato: mass, the Eucharist (the ceremony of Holy Communion)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech mšě, from Middle High German messe, from Old High German missa, from Ecclesiastical Latin missa, from Latin mittō, from Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂-.
Inherited from Old Czech nádherný. Reanalysed as nádhera + -ný.
Inherited from Old Czech opat, from Middle High German abbāt, from Latin abbās.
Inherited from Old Czech ortel, from Middle High German urteil.

parole.significato: pope (head of the Roman Catholic Church)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech papež, from Middle High German bābes, ultimately from Latin pāpa.
From Middle High German papier, from Old French papier.
Alteration of panchart, from Middle High German banchart.
Borrowed from Middle High German parchan.
Inherited from Old Czech pinta, ultimately from Middle High German Pinte.
From earlier puklice (“convex cap, cover”), from pukla (“convex ornament”), itself borrowed from Middle High German buckel (“circular metal ornament on a shield”).
Inherited from Old Czech pukla, from Middle High German buckel. Reanalysed as substantivised participle pukla from puknout.
Inherited from Old Czech pytel, borrowed from Middle High German piutel.
Inherited from Old Czech rada.
Inherited from Old Czech rej, borrowed from Middle High German reie.
Inherited from Old Czech rumpál, borrowed from Middle High German rollbaum.

parole.significato: square, an open space in a town
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech rynek, from Middle High German rinc (“town square”), originally “ring”, from Old High German ring. Doublet of ring (“boxing ring”).

parole.significato: square, an open space in a town
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle High German rinc (“a town square”), originally “a ring”.
Ultimately from Middle High German ritter (whence German Ritter). Compare Polish rycerz.
Inherited from Old Czech rám, from Middle High German ram, rame (German Rahmen).

parole.significato: grapevine, any member of the genus Vitis
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech réva, rév, in turn borrowed from Middle High German rëbe, see German Rebe.
Inherited from Old Czech rým (“verse”), Borrowed from Middle High German rīm.
Inherited from Old Czech rýž, from Middle High German rīs, from Latin orȳza.
From Middle High German reise + -ovat. Compare German Reise.
Inherited from Old Czech róžě, from Middle High German rôse, from Latin rosa.
Inherited from Old Czech samet.

parole.significato: dwarf, imp, gnome, sprite, goblin, gremlin
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle High German scrato.

parole.significato: to scold, to berate, to reproach
parole.testo: Probably from Old Czech spíleti, špíleti (“to joke, to tease”), from Middle High German spilen (German spielen).
Inherited from Old Czech taléř, from Middle High German teller (“plate”), from Middle French tailloir (“plate, cutting board”).

parole.significato: track (path or course laid out for a race, for exercise, etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech trata, borrowed from Middle High German trat.

parole.significato: to hit (to manage to touch in the right place)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle High German treffen.
Inherited from Old Czech troky, from Middle High German troc (German Trog).

parole.significato: to dare, have the courage (to do something)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle High German trūwen (German trauen), probably influenced by doufat.
Inherited from Old Czech truhla, from Middle High German truhe.

parole.significato: a chemical or food that is intended to kill a person or an animal
parole.testo: Derived from Middle High German hütterouch. Compare German Hüttenrauch.
Back-formation from váček, reinterpreted as a diminutive with the suffix -ek, while it actually originated in Middle High German wātsac.
Derived from Middle High German wal, from Latin vallum.
Inherited from Old Czech vikéř, from Middle High German wīchūs under the influence of arkýř. Doublet of výkuš.
Inherited from Old Czech ochle, borrowed from Middle High German hachel.
From vrh (“a throw”) + cáb; a partial calque of Middle High German wurfzabel = wurf (“a throw”) + zabel (“a board”), from Latin tabula.

The sense 'lock' is inherited from Proto-Slavic *zamъkъ. The sense 'manor house' is a semantic loan from Middle High German sloȥ (“lock, keep”) (cf. German Schloss), itself a semantic loan of Latin clūsa (“lock, fort, fortification”).

parole.significato: dumbbell, barbell (a piece of equipment used in weight training)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle High German schin (German Schiene). Influenced by činit.
Inherited from Old Czech činžě, from Middle High German zins.
Borrowed from Middle High German simz, modern Gesims (“cornice”).

parole.significato: sage (plant and savory spice; Salvia officinalis)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Czech šalvějě /šalvijě, from Middle High German salveie, ultimately from Latin salvia, derived from salvus (“well, unharmed”). See German Salbei for more.
Inherited from Old Czech šarvátka, from Middle High German scharwachte, from schar + wachte.
Borrowed from Middle High German schelme (“carrion”), for which see modern German Schelm.

parole.significato: to fence (to engage in the sport of fencing)
parole.testo: Derived from Middle High German schërmen (“to fence, to screen, to protect”), schirmen, from Old High German skirmen, + -ovat.
Borrowed from Middle High German schīden, schiden, scheiden (German scheiden).
Inherited from Old Czech šik (“order, tidiness”). From Middle High German schic, from Old High German *skicchen, from Proto-West Germanic *skikkijan (“to order, arrange”).

parole.significato: to squint (of eyes looking in different directions)
parole.testo: From Middle High German schilhen + -at.
Borrowed from Middle High German schindel.
Inherited from Old Czech šlechta, derived from Middle High German slahte, compare with German Geschlecht. See also Polish szlachta and Slovak šľachta.
Inherited from Old Czech špeh, which derived from Middle High German spëhen (“to spy”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *speḱ- (“to look”).
Inherited from Old Czech šumovati, from Middle High German schaumen, schoum.
Inherited from Old Czech švagr, from Middle High German swager.
Borrowed from Middle High German segenen, from Medieval Latin signō (whence also Polish żegnać, German segnen, English sain).
From žert + -ovat, from Middle High German serten. Compare Slovak žartovať, Polish żartować, Upper Sorbian žortować.
From Middle High German sold, from Old French solt, from Latin soldus, from solidum.

Inherited from Old Czech, a borrowing from Middle High German soldener, from Medieval Latin soldonerius, from Latin solidus. Compare Slovak žoldnier (“mercenary”), Polish żołnierz (“soldier, private”), modern German Söldner (“mercenary”).
From Old Czech žól (“the bottom of a mine”), borrowed from Middle High German sole, wherefrom German Sohle (“sole”). First attested in the 15th century.
Borrowed from Latin cunnus or from Middle High German kunt, from Old High German cunta, from Proto-Germanic *kuntǭ.
